question: How should the advance placement of warning signs be determined?
model_answer: Direct Answer: Advance placement of warning signs should be determined by providing drivers adequate Perception-Response Time (PRT), using the distances in Table 2C-3 (based on posted or 85th-percentile speed and the condition being warned of) applied with engineering judgment. In temporary traffic control zones, signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at distances that vary with roadway type, condition, and speed—per Table 6B-1—ranging from roughly 100 feet on low-speed urban streets to 1,000 feet or more (up to ½ mile or beyond) on freeways and expressways. These are recommended (Guidance) practices, not mandatory requirements. Guidance (recommended): - Warning signs should be placed so that they provide an adequate PRT; the distances in Table 2C-3 should be applied with engineering judgment, and the effectiveness of placement should be periodically evaluated under both day and night conditions. - Table 2C-3 provides advance placement distances by posted or 85th-percentile speed for Condition A (speed reduction and lane changing in heavy traffic) and Condition B (deceleration to a listed advisory speed); for signs with less than 6-inch legend or more than four words, a minimum of 100 feet should be added to provide adequate legibility. - In TTC zones, where highway conditions permit, warning signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at varying distances depending on roadway type, condition, and posted speed; where a series of two or more advance warning signs is used, the closest sign should be placed approximately 100 feet (low-speed urban streets) to 1,000 feet or more (freeways and expressways). - On freeways and expressways, advance warning sign placement should extend as far as ½ mile or more because drivers are conditioned to uninterrupted flow. - On urban streets, the effective placement of the nearest warning sign to the TTC zone should range from 4 to 8 times the speed limit in mph, with the high end used when speeds are relatively high; with two or more signs on higher-speed streets, the advance warning area should extend a greater distance (see Table 6B-1). - On rural highways, the effective placement of the first warning sign should be substantially longer—8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph—and the advance warning area should extend 1,500 feet or more for open highway conditions (see Table 6B-1). Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Table 2C-3 gives advance placement distances by speed (20–85 mph) for Condition A and Condition B (advisory speeds 0–80 mph), with footnotes on legibility adjustments and minimum 100-foot spacing. - [Image 2] Table 6B-1 shows warning sign minimum spacing dimensions A, B, and C by road type: 100 feet (urban low speed), 350 feet (urban high speed), 500 feet (rural), and 1,000/1,500/2,640 feet (expressway/freeway). - [Image 3] Page 193 shows Section 2C.04 (Placement of Warning Signs) with its Guidance paragraphs on PRT and Table 2C-3. - [Image 4] Page 839 shows Section 6H.02, Position of Advance Warning Signs, with the guidance on placement distances referencing Table 6B-1. - [Image 5] Page 197 shows Figure 2C-2 (Examples of Warning Signs for Changes in Horizontal Alignment), whose notes direct users to Table 2C-3 for advance placement distance guidelines. - [Image 6] Page 812 shows Section 6B.04 (Advance Warning Area) guidance on the 4–8 and 8–12 times-speed-limit rules and freeway/rural placement distances. Citations: - Section 2C.04 Guidance §5 (p.152) - Section 2C.04 Guidance §804 (p.153) - Section 6H.02 Guidance §1 (p.798) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §3 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §4 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §6 (p.771) - Table 2C-3 (p.152) - Table 6B-1 (p.773) - Page 193 - Page 839 - Page 197 - Page 812
gold_answer: Warning signs should be placed to provide adequate perception-response time. Table 2C-3 is an aid, but its distances should be applied with engineering judgment and can be adjusted for roadway features, other signing, and visibility.
